title: Phrasal verbs 5: on/off (2)
subtitle: carry on, get on, doze off, tell somebody off
summary: Use verb + on to mean continue, understand the three meanings of get on, and learn verbs with off such as doze off, rip off, show off and tell off.

lesson.heading: verb + on = continue
lesson.text: **go on** = continue. **go on doing** or **carry on doing** something = continue doing it. **go on with** or **carry on with** something = continue it.

examples.text: The party **went on** until 4 o'clock in the morning.
We can't **go on spending** money like this. We'll have nothing left soon.
I don't want to **carry on working** here. I'm going to look for another job.
Don't let me disturb you. Please **carry on with** what you're doing.

lesson.heading: keep on doing, drive on, walk on
lesson.text: **keep on doing** (or **keep doing**) something = do it continuously or repeatedly. **drive on / walk on / play on** = continue driving / walking / playing etc.

examples.text: He **keeps on criticising** me. It's not fair! or He **keeps criticising** me.
Shall we stop at this petrol station or shall we **drive on** to the next one?

lesson.heading: get on - three meanings
rows: How are you **getting on** in your new job? (= How is it going?)
Joanne and Karen don't **get on**. They're always arguing. / Richard **gets on** well **with** his neighbours.
continue something you have to do, usually after an interruption
I must **get on with** my work. I have a lot to do.

lesson.heading: verb + off: doze off, finish off, go off
lesson.text: **doze off / drop off / nod off** = fall asleep. **finish something off** = do the last part of it. **go off** = make an alarm sound.

examples.text: I **dozed off** during the lecture. It was very boring.
*A:* Have you finished painting the kitchen? *B:* Nearly. I'll **finish it off** tomorrow.
Did you hear the alarm **go off**?

lesson.heading: put off, rip off, show off, tell off
lesson.text: **put somebody off** (doing) something = make them not want it or not want to do it. **rip somebody off** / **be ripped off** = cheat somebody / be cheated. **show off** = try to impress people with your ability or knowledge. **tell somebody off** = speak angrily to them because they did something wrong.

examples.text: We wanted to go to the exhibition, but we were **put off** by the long queue.
examples.note: = we didn't go because of the long queue

examples.text: What **put you off** applying for the job? Was the salary too low?
Did you really pay £2,000 for that painting? I think you were **ripped off**.
Look at that boy on the bike riding with no hands. He's just **showing off**.
Clare's mother **told her off** for wearing dirty shoes in the house.

lesson.text: Three ways to fall asleep by accident: **doze off**, **drop off**, **nod off** - all mean the same.

exercises.prompt: 'I nodded off.' What does this mean?
exercises.explanation: nod off = doze off = drop off = fall asleep.

exercises.prompt: 'We were ripped off.' What does this mean?
exercises.explanation: be ripped off = be cheated, pay too much.

exercises.prompt: Match each phrasal verb with its meaning.

pairs.right: speak angrily to them for doing something wrong
do the last part of it

exercises.prompt: I'm not ready to go home yet. I have a few things to ___.
exercises.explanation: finish something off = do the last part of it.

exercises.prompt: The fire alarm ___ and everybody had to leave the building.
exercises.explanation: go off = make an alarm sound.

exercises.prompt: 'Shall I stop the car here?' 'No, ___ a bit further.'
exercises.explanation: drive on / carry on / go on = continue driving.

exercises.prompt: What does get on mean in each sentence?

items.text: How are you getting on in your new job?
Joanne and Karen don't get on. They're always arguing.
I must get on with my work. I have a lot to do.
Richard gets on well with his neighbours.
Emma is enjoying her course. She's getting on very well.
I've just had a coffee break, and now I must get on with my work.

exercises.statement: Ben was told off by his boss for being late for work repeatedly.
exercises.explanation: Correct. tell somebody off = speak angrily to them because they did something wrong.

exercises.statement: We decided not to go to the concert. We were put on by the cost of the tickets.
exercises.explanation: We were put off by the cost of the tickets. put somebody off = make them not want to do something.

exercises.prompt: Some children at the next table in the restaurant were behaving very badly. Ask why their parents did nothing.
exercises.answer: Why didn't their parents tell them off?
exercises.explanation: tell them off - the pronoun goes between tell and off.

exercises.prompt: 'Is Kate good at making decisions?' 'No, she isn't. She ___ changing her mind.'
exercises.explanation: keep on doing or keep doing something = do it repeatedly.

exercises.prompt: 'Is Gary going to retire soon?' 'No, he likes his job and wants to ___ working.'
exercises.explanation: carry on / go on / keep on doing something = continue doing it.
